On the night of Ramchandra Ray’s escape, Udayaditya overpowers Sitaram: he orders the door opened, draws his sword when Sitaram cites the ban on leaving, and Sitaram, refusing to fight the man who twice saved his life, yields his weapon and asks to be bound so he can face the Maharaj the next day; Udayaditya disarms and ties him and goes on. On the night of Udayaditya’s own escape, the roles reverse: Sitaram opens the prison during the fire, pulls Udayaditya out, and leads him away while Udayaditya, helpless after long confinement, only asks where to go and follows.

Pratapaditya first ordered two Pathans to kill Basanta Ray at the Simultali inn on the way to Jessore; they failed to do it. Basanta Ray is finally killed at Raigarh by Pratapaditya’s order, when Muktiyar Khan has Abdul cut him down with a sword during evening prayers.
In the Jessore palace inner quarters while disguised as a middle-aged woman, and in the Chandradwip palace chamber while appearing as the court jester.
Mangala (Rukmini) prepares and supplies poison disguised as medicine, which kills Surma.
The Maharaj remarries, leaving Vibha no place in her own kingdom or palace.

Rukmini takes the signet ring from Udayaditya after confronting him. Sitaram and Bhagavat then use that ring—bearing the Yubaraj’s name—to seal a forged petition supposedly from Udayaditya accusing Pratapaditya of treason before the Emperor. Bhagavat delivers the sealed petition to Pratapaditya as proof of Udayaditya’s treachery, and on that evidence Pratapaditya orders him imprisoned.

Ramchandra’s midnight escape leads to the dismissal of the guards Sitaram and Bhagavat. Udayaditya then supports them with stipends; when Pratapaditya forbids this, Surma continues the aid in secret. Discovery of those secret stipends prompts Pratapaditya’s order that Surma be sent to her paternal home.

The song voices Basanta Ray’s loneliness and bereavement—those once dear to him are gone, leaving only emptiness—and he can no longer sing with joy. He sings it alone at sunset in Raigarh in solitary melancholy, and again in Jessore while holding Vibha’s hand after finding the household emptied of its loved ones.

Because she failed to stop the escape, Udayaditya fled to Raigarh with Basanta Ray; she then exposed the truth to Pratapaditya, who sent Muktiyar Khan with a death sentence for the King of Raigarh, and she herself guided the soldiers to capture Udayaditya so that order could be carried out and Basanta Ray killed.

Pratapaditya received Ramchandra with cool indifference—no joy or haste, a bare greeting, immediate attention to other business, and a curt dismissal as “my boy.” Later, in his own court, Ramchandra and his courtiers daily mock Pratapaditya as low-born and inferior, treating any comparison with their king as audacity and the marriage as a favor that already redeemed Jessore’s line.
She settles on the outskirts of Jessore as Mangala and, asked for a love-charm for Udayaditya, prepares poison that kills Surma.

Udayaditya’s early wish not to have been born crown prince ends when, brought before Pratapaditya as a prisoner, he renounces the throne: he swears before Ma-Kali never to claim any of Jessore’s kingdom, names Samaraditya heir, and leaves for Kashi as an ascetic.

Nayanchand, afraid to deliver it to Pratapaditya, gives the letter to the Mahishi instead. She later shows it to Basanta Ray, who advises her to announce that Ramchandra has written requesting Vibha be sent to Chandradwip. The Mahishi does so, and Vibha is told and believes that her husband has summoned her.

Pratapaditya blocks the palace canal with large sal logs to trap the boat, but Rammohan and his men haul it up and over the barrier while the guards’ pursuit is delayed and bungled, so the boat reaches the Bhairav.

When forced to leave Udayaditya, Basanta Ray abandons his sitar and vows never to play it again; later, alone and desolate over the prince’s fate, he keeps the instrument but says its strings are broken and it can no longer be tuned—his lost music mirroring a spirit emptied of joy.

Earlier he was known for involving himself in subjects’ affairs and opposing oppression even against the king’s wishes; after Surma’s death a blind fear of Pratapaditya strips him of that courage, so he hesitates, turns back from intervening, and no longer protects or aids the oppressed.
By freeing Udayaditya from prison during the fire.
He carries Ramchandra on his back down a rope of knotted sheets from the palace roof into a waiting boat, and later lifts the unconscious Vibha into a palanquin and takes her to the boat.

In Jessore she is elaborately adorned by her mother—thick gold bangles, a huge diamond bracelet, a large nose ring, and a carefully restyled coiffure—and appears as a shy, joyously dressed princess. In Chandradwip she refuses a queen’s palanquin, goes out dressed as a common woman or beggar, enters the palace like a maidservant, and is taken for a beggar-woman seeking alms.

After Surma’s death the window is a place of absence and mourning: he sits there leaving her seat empty, seeing the same moonlight, garden, and breeze, and hoping she might still appear. In the prison the small window becomes a symbol of hope and freedom: through it he watches the sky and birds and believes his cage will one day break; only there does he feel naturally free, while away from it he sees only darkness and forgets liberation.

Sitaram, penniless but stylish, courts Rukmini for her beauty and silver, borrows from her with flattery and endearments, and turns their money dealings into a secret scheme. When Udayaditya is imprisoned, he storms her house, curses her, and threatens to ruin her and free the prince; she seethes that the Yubaraj is hers alone and vows to stop him. After helping the escape and staging the prison fire, he goes to loot her house, thinking her dead. He finds her alive, wet and ashen; she swears to burn him and the Yubaraj before she dies and fetches a curved blade. He flees; she strikes the empty floor and later names him to the king as the conspirator.

Sitaram first uses the guardhouse fire as a distraction: while guards flee and chaos erupts, he opens the prison and leads Udayaditya out under the pretext that the prison itself is burning. The plan then becomes a cover-up. Loyal men keep the blaze going by sabotaging firefighting, then set the empty cell alight. Sitaram throws bones, a skull, and Udayaditya’s sword into the flames, stages reports of screams and a collapsed roof, and spreads the story that the Yubaraj died in the fire—buying time while the escape is completed.
He discounts the rescue as owed and self-interested, believing Udayaditya acted mainly for his sister rather than for him, and joins his court in ridiculing Udayaditya.

Pratapaditya first dismisses the Emperor of Delhi as no real threat and forbids the minister from using that name to deter him. Later a forged petition is written as if Prince Udayaditya were charging Pratapaditya with treason before the Emperor to seize the kingdom, stamped with the Yubaraj’s seal, and delivered to Pratapaditya as intercepted on its way to Delhi; that supposed appeal to the Emperor turns the dismissed specter into the proof used against his son.

While Surma lived, Vibha would slip away to have her hair dressed to her own liking by Surma, so that the coiffure itself marked Surma’s intimate presence and care in the Jessore palace. After Surma’s death, Vibha still sat waiting as if Surma would come at any moment to braid it; the hair stayed unbraided, and later appeared unkempt, turning that same daily ritual into the clearest sign of Surma’s irreversible absence.
